title: Blood Management Strategies in Placenta Accreta Spectrum.
abstract: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) presents a major challenge in obstetric care because attempted placental separation may result in rapid and life-threatening hemorrhage. As PAS is often suspected before delivery, there is an opportunity to identify correctable risks and prepare for anticipated blood loss. This narrative review examines blood-management strategies throughout the antenatal, intraoperative, and postoperative periods. A targeted narrative search of PubMed and PubMed Central, supplemented by searches of journal and publisher websites, was conducted for literature available through September 2026. Antenatal management focuses on identifying and treating maternal anemia, referring patients to experienced centers, and developing a multidisciplinary delivery plan. Perioperative preparation includes coordination with the transfusion service, timely access to appropriate blood components, clear criteria for activating a major obstetric hemorrhage protocol, and defined responsibilities for each team member. Blood-product preparation should be individualized according to the severity suggested by prenatal imaging and the anticipated anatomical extent of placental invasion, ranging from suspected accreta to increta or percreta. Key intraoperative blood-conservation measures include intraoperative cell salvage and timely administration of tranexamic acid when clinically indicated, particularly during significant hemorrhage. Viscoelastic hemostatic testing, fibrinogen-directed therapy, and selected interventional radiology procedures may also contribute to individualized management. However, evidence supporting these interventions remains inconsistent and is frequently derived from observational studies, expert consensus, or broader obstetric hemorrhage populations rather than PAS-specific randomized trials. Consequently, blood-management plans should reflect the anticipated severity of PAS, the patient's clinical condition, and the expertise and resources available at the treating institution. A structured and individualized approach linking antenatal optimization, multidisciplinary preparation, timely hemorrhage control, and postoperative surveillance may support safer and more efficient care for patients with PAS.

title: When Hypercapnia Misleads: A Case of Respiratory-Onset Motor Neuron Disease.
abstract: Motor neuron disease (MND) most commonly presents with limb or bulbar weakness; however, a minority of patients present with respiratory-onset disease, posing significant diagnostic challenges. We report the case of a 78-year-old woman with a background of small airways disease and rheumatoid arthritis not requiring treatment for many years, who presented with a two-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, unintentional weight loss, and functional decline. Before diagnosis, she underwent extensive investigation across primary and secondary care, including chest radiography, spirometry, computed tomography imaging, and ear, nose, and throat specialist assessment, without a unifying diagnosis being established. On admission, venous blood gas demonstrated compensated hypercapnia, which was attributed to obstructive airways disease. She subsequently developed hypercapnic respiratory failure, and a clinical diagnosis of MND was made on the basis of generalised muscle wasting, fasciculations, brisk lower-limb reflexes, and electromyography findings. Non-invasive ventilation was initiated with significant clinical improvement. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of respiratory-onset MND, the risk of anchoring bias in the interpretation of biochemical markers, and the importance of considering neuromuscular causes when respiratory symptoms are disproportionate to radiological and biochemical findings.

title: Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome Mimicking Ulcerative Colitis: A Case Report.
abstract: Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (SRUS) is a benign rectal disorder associated with abnormal defecation and mucosal prolapse. Its clinical and endoscopic features may mimic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We report the case of a 28-year-old woman with longstanding obstructed defecation who presented with recurrent bloody mucus discharge and severe iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL), which was treated with intravenous iron infusions. C-reactive protein was normal, whereas fecal calprotectin was markedly elevated. Initial colonoscopy showed erythematous and congested mucosa extending from the anal verge to 20 cm, with a large ulcer, raising suspicion of ulcerative colitis. However, the initial biopsies were inconclusive. Following clinical worsening, repeat colonoscopy revealed a 5-cm elevated rectal lesion with central ulceration. Histological examination demonstrated epithelial loss, granulation tissue, villiform crypt changes, and characteristic fibromuscular hyperplasia of the lamina propria, establishing the diagnosis of SRUS. Magnetic resonance defecography revealed an anterior rectocele and internal rectal prolapse, while anorectal manometry demonstrated dyssynergic defecation. Conservative measures and biofeedback provided incomplete improvement, with persistent rectal bleeding. Given the documented internal rectal prolapse and refractory symptoms, laparoscopic ventral rectopexy was performed, resulting in a favorable postoperative clinical course with marked symptomatic improvement and normalization of hemoglobin to 13.7 g/dL. SRUS should be considered when inflammatory-appearing rectal lesions are not supported by histological evidence of IBD, particularly in patients with obstructed defecation.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Automated Analysis and Interpretation of Intravascular Ultrasound in Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) leads to considerable morbidity and mortality worldwide. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is an imaging modality to guide percutaneous coronary intervention; however, it requires time-consuming, expert-dependent manual analysis. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly used for IVUS analysis, but there is limited evidence on its diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility. This review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness of AI for automated IVUS analysis of coronary arteries. The research protocol was prospectively registered (PROSPERO, CRD420261454806) and followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic reviews. PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through July 23, 2026, and July 26, 2026, respectively, for publications assessing AI, machine learning, or deep learning algorithms for the automated analysis of coronary IVUS, including segmentation of structures, identification of plaque types, and quantitative measurements. Two reviewers independently screened and selected eligible studies and extracted the data. The risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) and visualized using robvis, and the GRADE approach was used to rate the certainty of evidence. Of the 802 records identified (PubMed, n = 216; Cochrane CENTRAL, n = 586), eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in this review. They reported on the performance of convolutional neural networks, U-Net/U-Net++, Efficient-UNet, DeepLabv3+-based models, and gradient boosting in segmenting lumen, vessel, plaque, and stent in coronary IVUS. The Dice similarity coefficient ranged from 0.67 to 0.97, and the intersection over union for segmentation (including Jaccard similarity) ranged from 0.66 to 0.97, with the best performance for lumen and vessel segmentation and the poorest for stent and calcium. The sensitivity and specificity ranged from 62% to 90% and 88% to 99%, respectively, with the correlation to expert assessment generally above 0.9. Overall, the risk of bias was mainly related to patient selection (five out of eight studies) and the reference standard (three out of eight studies), and none of the studies was rated as having a high risk of bias. Due to between-study heterogeneity in the tasks, reference standards, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not performed, and the certainty of evidence was rated as low. The current evidence suggests that AI-based methods have good potential for analyzing coronary IVUS with acceptable accuracy, which could be helpful for high-throughput IVUS interpretation in clinical practice. They appear to perform best at segmenting lumen and vessel structures and worst at segmenting stent and calcium. However, due to the overall low certainty of evidence from these mostly retrospective studies, their use should be limited to complementing the work of experts in cardiovascular medicine.

title: Endoscopic Excision of a C5 Osteoid Osteoma With Intraoperative Computed Tomography.
abstract: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone tumor characterized by nocturnal pain, with a predilection for teenage male patients. A 15-year-old boy presented with a two-month history of neck pain and was referred to our hospital, where imaging studies revealed an osteoid osteoma of the cervical vertebra. As he was preparing for a national basketball tournament and wished to return to sports as soon as possible, minimally invasive surgery was performed to excise the tumor using an endoscopic technique with intraoperative computed tomography, which confirmed that the extent of excision matched the preoperative surgical plan. His pain improved immediately postoperatively, and he was able to return to sports three months after surgery. At two years postoperatively, follow-up imaging showed no recurrence, progressive spinal malalignment, or spondylolisthesis.

title: Mandibular Canal Morphometry and Anatomical Variations Using Cone-Beam Computed Tomography in a North Indian Population: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Introduction The present study aimed to evaluate the morphology, dimensions, anatomical variations, and spatial characteristics of the mandibular canal (MC) in a North Indian population using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). The associations between MC characteristics and sex, age, and laterality were also assessed to identify clinically relevant patterns of anatomical variation. Materials and methods This retrospective database observational study was conducted using 400 CBCT scans of adults aged ≥18 years between June 2024 and May 2025. The scans were evaluated using multiplanar and curved planar reconstructions. MC course, length, vertical and horizontal diameters, buccolingual position, anterior loop, bifid and trifid canals, and accessory mental foramina were assessed. Two calibrated observers independently evaluated the scans, with repeated assessments performed to establish measurement reliability. Differences according to sex and side, as well as associations with age, were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to account for bilateral observations. Multinomial logistic GEE were used for categorical canal patterns. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results Among the 400 participants, 220 were males and 180 were females, with a mean age of 42.6 ± 12.1 years. Males demonstrated significantly greater canal length, vertical diameter, horizontal diameter, and anterior loop length than females. Bifid canals were significantly more common in males than in females. The ascending canal morphology was the most common pattern, followed by catenary and straight configurations, with no significant sex differences. No significant right-left differences were observed in canal dimensions or anatomical variants. The canal was predominantly centrally positioned buccolingually across all tooth regions, ranging from 67.5% in the second premolar region to 76.0% in the third molar region. Increasing age was significantly associated with reduced canal length, whereas other measured characteristics showed no significant age-related associations. Conclusion MC anatomy demonstrates substantial morphological variability, with significant differences related to sex and age but limited bilateral asymmetry. CBCT assessment provides a detailed characterization of canal dimensions, course, and anatomical variants. Recognition of these variations is important for individualized preoperative evaluation and for minimizing neurovascular complications during mandibular surgical procedures.

title: Bilateral Adrenal Masses, Extreme Catecholamine Excess, and Hypercalcitoninemia With Metastatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasia: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
abstract: A 40-year-old man presented with back pain, urinary retention, mild unilateral weakness, weight loss, hypercalcemia, and newly recognized hypertension. During the early admission, blood pressure became markedly labile, reaching 225/106 mmHg. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated approximately 10-cm bilateral heterogeneous adrenal masses and diffuse lytic skeletal metastases. Biochemical testing showed profound catecholamine excess, including urine metanephrine/creatinine 42,040 µg/g creatinine (reference range: 29-158 µg/g), normetanephrine/creatinine 6,079 µg/g creatinine (reference range: 53-659 µg/g), and vanillylmandelic acid/creatinine 212 mg/g creatinine (reference range: 1.1-4.1 mg/g). Serum calcitonin was 4,680 pg/mL (reference ≤8.4), with carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) 239 ng/mL (reference <3.8 ng/mL for a non-smoker). Expert review of a bone biopsy showed a metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, WHO grade 3 (2017), with Ki-67 approximately 40%. The tumor expressed chromogranin, synaptophysin, pancytokeratin, thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1), CEA, paired box 8 (PAX8), and cytokeratin (CK) 7 but was negative for calcitonin, thyroglobulin, CK20, GATA3, and S100. The case illustrates clinicopathologic discordance: the biochemical phenotype strongly favored pheochromocytoma, whereas metastatic-site histology did not establish the primary site.

title: A Brain Metastasis in Search of Its Origin: Occult Primary Non-small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: We present a case of a 67-year-old man who presented with right-sided hemiparesis and headache and was found to have a solitary left temporoparietal cerebral lesion on MRI, initially favoring a primary brain tumor. Further workup was unremarkable and the patient underwent surgical resection of the cerebral lesion. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry favored a metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma, though imaging scans showed no primary lung lesion. Subsequent PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic mediastinal, hilar, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, consistent with occult primary non-small cell lung cancer. The patient underwent stereotactic gamma knife radiotherapy to the resection bed, followed by systemic chemotherapy with cisplatin and vinorelbine. At the time of writing, two of three planned chemotherapy cycles had been completed, with radiological response assessment scheduled after completion of the treatment. This case adds to the limited literature on occult primary non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and supports early tissue diagnosis as key to appropriate management.

title: Lower Back Pain As the Initial Manifestation of Primary Follicular B-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma of the Bone Marrow: A Case Report.
abstract: Follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-NHL) is a malignant disease of the lymphatic system that primarily affects the lymph nodes. The primary presentation of follicular B-NHL in the bone is extremely rare. The patient, a 53-year-old woman, developed non-radiating lower back pain at the age of 52. Diagnostic evaluation via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) revealed a solid intraosseous mass in the L3 vertebral body, an L2 compression fracture, and extensive metastatic disease involving the ribs, vertebral bodies, ilium, and cranial vault. Three months after the onset of lower back pain, a CT-guided biopsy of the ilium confirmed the presence of follicular B-NHL lymphoma cells. These cells tested positive for CD10, BCL6, and BCL2, as well as for the minimal residual disease marker t(14;18). Cranial MRI showed osseous lesions in the cranial vault but no intra-axial lesions. No extraosseous metastases were detected. Risk stratification indicated stage IVA, Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (FLIPI): 4-5, and FLIPI2: 3. Six cycles (one per month) of therapy with rituximab, bendamustine, and intravenous immunoglobulins proved ineffective after five months. Twelve months after symptom onset, the lymphoma progressed and transformed into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Various attempts to treat the DLBCL were also unsuccessful. Twenty months after the onset of lower back pain, the patient died of sepsis. In summary, this case demonstrates that follicular B-NHL can initially involve only the bones and manifest solely as lumbar back pain. In summary, this case demonstrates that follicular B-NHL can initially involve only the bones and manifest solely as lumbar back pain. Despite chemotherapy, symptoms may worsen, and B-NHL may transform into fatal DLBCL.

title: A Volumetric Anatomy-Aware, Prompt-Guided Adaptation Framework for the Segment Anything Model in Head and Neck Radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Head and neck (H&N) radiotherapy planning requires accurate segmentation of numerous organs at risk (OARs), yet many critical structures, such as the optic nerves, chiasm, and cochleae, are small, poorly contrasted on CT, and prone to high inter-observer variability in manual contouring. Recent foundation models like Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its 3D medical variants (SAM-Med3D) offer prompt-based, interactive segmentation, but their real-world utility for H&N small OARs is hindered by unreliable prompt sources and unstable performance on fine anatomical targets. To address these issues, this work proposes an anatomy-aware prompt generation and prompt-guided adaptation tailored specifically for small-structure segmentation to improve both precision and automation feasibility. Purpose To address these challenges, we developed a domain-adapted framework, SAM-FT-HN, by fine-tuning a volumetric SAM backbone (SAM-Med3D) for automated delineation of H&N OARs in radiotherapy planning. Our approach incorporates a coarse-to-fine pipeline in which a lightweight localization network automatically generates organ-specific prompts and candidate regions, followed by a fine-tuned volumetric SAM backbone for refinement. We further introduced task-specific strategies including region-of-interest (ROI)-guided tiny-organ enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration to improve performance on small structures. The primary objective is to develop and evaluate a fully automated, anatomy-aware adaptation of SAM-Med3D for H&N OAR segmentation, with a secondary objective of improving small-organ segmentation. We systematically compared SAM-FT-HN against baseline SAM-Med3D and nnUNet models quantitatively and qualitatively. Methods We used an institutional H&N CT dataset of 211 patients with manual delineations of 23 OARs, standardized for training, validation, and testing. Eighty percent of cases were used for training and validation, and twenty percent for testing. The testing phase used CT volumes only, and ground-truth masks were used solely for metric calculation. A coarse localization network was trained to generate automatic prompts and ROI candidates. SAM-FT-HN was fine-tuned using task-specific adaptations, and small-organ refinement was performed using ROI-guided enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration. nnUNet was trained using its automated configuration pipeline. Performance was evaluated using overlap and boundary metrics. Results For large OARs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice of 0.814 compared with 0.791 for nnUNet and substantially higher than SAM-Med3D (0.609). For small organs, SAM-FT-HN improved the mean Dice from 0.300 to 0.669 compared with SAM-Med3D and reduced HD95 by approximately 65%, although nnUNet remained higher in average small-organ Dice (0.720). Overall, across all organs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice score of 0.770, compared with 0.769 for nnUNet. Overall, SAM-FT-HN showed no statistically significant difference from nnUNet in the patient-level analysis, while substantially outperforming the original SAM-Med3D baseline. Conclusion Fine-tuning a foundation model with anatomy-aware automatic prompting, coarse-to-fine localization, and adaptive thresholding markedly improves small-organ segmentation, substantially mitigating a key limitation of the original foundation model. SAM-FT-HN offers a competitive approach for H&N radiotherapy contouring, with potential for future adaptive workflows.

title: Multilevel Lumbar Epidural Angiolipoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Spinal angiolipomas are rare benign tumors composed of mature adipose tissue and vascular elements, most commonly located in the thoracic epidural space. Lumbar involvement is considerably less frequent, and variable proportions of adipose and vascular tissue may result in atypical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics and diagnostic uncertainty. We report the case of a 36-year-old woman with an approximately one-year history of persistent low back pain associated with subjective bilateral lower-extremity weakness despite a preserved neurological examination. An initial non-contrast lumbar MRI was interpreted as showing no significant abnormality other than minimal degenerative changes; however, retrospective review revealed a subtle posterior epidural lesion. Because of persistent symptoms, further investigation with contrast-enhanced MRI was performed, demonstrating an elongated epidural lesion extending from L1 to L3, predominantly involving the posterior and right posterolateral epidural space with associated foraminal extension. The lesion demonstrated areas of low T1 signal intensity and intense homogeneous contrast enhancement. The patient underwent L1-L3 laminoplasty and gross-total resection. Intraoperatively, the lesion had a macroscopically adipose appearance and was moderately vascular. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature adipose tissue admixed with numerous vascular channels, confirming the diagnosis of spinal angiolipoma. Postoperatively, pain and subjective lower-extremity weakness improved without new neurological deficits, and early postoperative MRI showed no evidence of residual or recurrent tumor. This case highlights the variable imaging appearance of lumbar spinal angiolipomas and the value of correlating MRI characteristics with intraoperative and histopathological findings, particularly in enhancing epidural lesions without a predominantly fatty appearance.

title: Fever and Painful Skin Lesions: When to Consider Sweet's Syndrome.
abstract: Sweet's syndrome is an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis characterised by fever, neutrophilia, and painful cutaneous lesions. We describe a case of a 31-year-old male admitted with a two-week history of fever up to 39°C and painful erythematous papules, scattered and coalescing into plaques over the trunk and limbs, together with pustules on an erythematous base over the palms and dorsum of the hands. No relevant epidemiological exposure or recent drug exposure was identified. Investigation showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h, leucocytosis of 14,380/µL with 77% neutrophils and no eosinophilia, and a C-reactive protein of 1.21 mg/dL. Liver and renal function, albumin, lactate dehydrogenase, serum iron, ferritin, and serum protein electrophoresis were normal, and a respiratory viral panel was negative. Blood, urine, and pustule cultures, an interferon-gamma release assay, and serology for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, hepatitis A, B, C, and E viruses, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus were negative, as was an autoantibody panel. Serum immunoglobulin A was below the detection limit (<0.07 g/L) before corticosteroid therapy and on all repeat measurements, including after treatment had been discontinued, with normal immunoglobulin G and M, and IgG-based coeliac serology was negative. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed no abnormalities. A skin biopsy demonstrated intraepidermal blisters and a superficial perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis, spongiform pustules, or psoriasiform changes. The clinical and laboratory criteria for classical Sweet's syndrome were fulfilled, and the histology was compatible with, although not classical for, the syndrome. Prednisolone 60 mg/day (approximately 0.6 mg/kg/day) was started on clinical suspicion of the syndrome. After one week, the fever had resolved, but the lesions worsened slightly, prompting escalation to 100 mg/day (approximately 1 mg/kg/day), after which they regressed progressively and resolved completely within three weeks of dose escalation, with normalisation of the leucocyte count. Corticosteroids were tapered and discontinued before the three-month assessment, at which there was no relapse and no evidence of malignancy. This case illustrates three practical points: an acral pustular morphology does not exclude the diagnosis; early worsening under corticosteroid therapy may reflect an initial dose insufficient for body weight rather than an incorrect diagnosis, once infection has been rigorously excluded; and the coexisting finding of selective immunoglobulin A deficiency carries independent implications for coeliac disease screening and long-term follow-up.

title: Managing Severe Proximal Femoral Fibrous Dysplasia in a Young Adult Using Hemiarthroplasty in a Resource-Constrained Healthcare System: A Case Report.
abstract: Fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur may lead to progressive deformity, pain, and pathological fractures, with shepherd's crook deformity representing one of its most severe manifestations. Although valgus osteotomy with intramedullary fixation is considered the preferred surgical treatment, extensive bone destruction and limited healthcare resources may preclude conventional reconstruction. We present a case of severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia successfully managed with bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty in a resource-constrained healthcare setting. A 25-year-old man presented with progressive left hip pain, severe proximal femoral deformity, and impaired ambulation. Radiographic evaluation demonstrated lateral bowing of the proximal femur, while histopathological examination following core biopsy confirmed fibrous dysplasia. Internal fixation using an intramedullary nail was initially planned; however, intraoperative findings revealed extensive fibro-osseous replacement, severely compromised bone quality, and inadequate cortical support, making stable fixation technically impossible. Because more complex reconstructive procedures were not covered by the national health insurance system, a bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty, augmented with plate fixation of the osteotomized fragments, was performed as a salvage procedure. The postoperative course was uneventful, with marked pain relief, improved gait, and satisfactory functional recovery at 10 months of follow-up (Oxford Hip Score 34/48). Conventional fixation for shepherd's crook deformity requires adequate residual cortical bone to achieve stable implant fixation. In cases with extensive cortical destruction and bone stock too thin to support reliable press-fit fixation, cemented hemiarthroplasty may represent a practical alternative. Preservation of the native acetabulum may also reduce postoperative instability while providing satisfactory functional outcomes. Bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty may be an effective salvage option for selected patients with severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia when conventional fixation is technically unfeasible, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare systems.

title: Phyllodes Tumors of the Breast in 2026: A Contemporary Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Surgical Margins, Prognosis, and Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Phyllodes tumors of the breast are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms characterized by significant heterogeneity regarding morphology, biological behavior, and clinical outcome. This review summarizes current developments in the diagnosis, histopathological and molecular classification, therapeutic management, and emerging technologies associated with phyllodes tumors of the breast. A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar, focusing on publications from the 2000-2026 period. The literature search covered publications from January 1, 2000, to September 30, 2026, and was last updated on September 30, 2026. Mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging contribute to preoperative assessment, although significant diagnostic overlap with fibroadenomas persists. Core needle biopsy is a key diagnostic tool, yet lesion heterogeneity can limit the accuracy of histological classification. Advances in molecular pathology have identified mutations and pathways associated with the progression and aggressiveness of phyllodes tumors, though these have not yet replaced morphological assessment. Surgical excision with negative margins remains the primary therapeutic approach, while the risk of local recurrence depends on histological grade, surgical margins, and other clinicopathological characteristics. Radiotherapy in phyllodes tumors of the breast appears to offer benefits primarily regarding local control in selected high-risk cases. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, radiomics, and digital pathology, are proving to be promising tools for diagnosis, grading, and prognostic assessment. Overall, modern management of phyllodes tumors of the breast is shifting toward more personalized and multifactorial approaches.

title: When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1.
abstract: Silent somatotroph adenomas are uncommon pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs) of the PIT1 lineage that express growth hormone (GH) immunohistochemically but without biochemical evidence of acromegaly. We report the case of a 32-year-old male patient referred with recurrent epistaxis, headache, right-sided diplopia, and third cranial nerve palsy. Clinical examination revealed acromegaloid features including frontal bossing, spade-like hands, and coarse facies, which were strongly suggestive of longstanding GH excess. However, preoperative insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was paradoxically low at 13.1 nmol/L (reference range 15.5-33.1 nmol/L), creating a striking clinical-biochemical discordance. MRI demonstrated a giant sellar and suprasellar mass with chiasmal compression, right cavernous sinus invasion, and extension into the paranasal sinuses. The patient underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal resection. Neuropathology confirmed a densely granulated PIT1-lineage somatotroph adenoma with scattered GH positivity, diffuse Pit-1 staining, and a Ki-67 index below 2%. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by silent somatotroph adenomas, underscores the limitations of biochemical assessment alone, and reinforces the essential role of histopathology and immunohistochemistry in establishing a definitive diagnosis. Long-term endocrine and neurosurgical surveillance is strongly recommended given the potential for phenotypic transformation to a functioning acromegaly syndrome.

title: Ovarian Myxoma in a Patient With Missed Abortion: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
abstract: Ovarian myxoma is a rare benign mesenchymal tumor. It can be completely asymptomatic and is difficult to differentiate from other ovarian masses before surgery and final histopathology. We report a case of a 28-year-old primigravida who presented with a missed abortion at 11 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasonography incidentally showed a 6.5 × 5.7 cm complex solid-cystic right adnexal lesion in the pouch of Douglas. She was asymptomatic from the mass. After dilatation and evacuation for missed abortion, the patient was evaluated for an ovarian mass, and tumor markers were found negative. Repeat ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous lesion with coarse hyperechoic foci and posterior acoustic shadowing, suggesting a right ovarian teratoma. The patient was taken for laparotomy, wherein an 8 × 8 cm solid-cystic mass was found in the right ovary, and right ovarian cystectomy was done. Intraoperative scrape cytology came back negative for malignancy and showed columnar cells, squamous cells, and mature adipose tissue, which favored a benign cystic teratoma. Histopathology showed a thick collagenous capsule and stellate cells in abundant myxoid stroma without atypia. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for vimentin and negative for desmin and cytokeratin. The final diagnosis was ovarian myxoma. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. There was no recurrence at one-year follow-up. This case shows that ovarian myxoma can mimic a mature cystic teratoma on imaging, gross examination, and cytology, and that the final diagnosis depends on histopathological examination (HPE) supported by immunohistochemistry.

title: Diffuse-Type Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Flexor Hallucis Longus Tendon Sheath: A Case Report.
abstract: The synovium can be the primary site for the development of various benign or malignant tumors. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, is a benign but locally aggressive synovial neoplasm occurring in localized and diffuse forms. The localized form predominantly affects the hand, whereas the diffuse form mainly involves large joints; involvement of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath is rare. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the principal modality for demonstrating the hemosiderin deposits characteristic of this lesion, although histopathology remains necessary for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment. We report the case of a 24-year-old man with 10 months of right ankle pain, related to a diffuse-type TGCT involving the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and adjacent ankle joints. Radiographs initially showed soft-tissue filling of Kager's triangle. Computed tomography arthrography demonstrated synovial thickening but was nonspecific; MRI then revealed the characteristic findings, and histopathology confirmed the diagnosis. This report aims to raise awareness of this rare location and its associated diagnostic pitfalls.

title: Congenital Hypoplasia of the C1 Posterior Arch Masquerading as Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Report.
abstract: Hypoplasia of the C1 posterior arch is a rare congenital anomaly, classified using the Currarino system into subtypes A through E depending on the extent and nature of arch deficiency. The majority of cases are incidental radiological findings; symptomatic presentations causing cervical myelopathy are exceptionally uncommon and not well represented in the surgical literature. In such cases, the absence of established management guidelines renders clinical decision-making particularly challenging. We present a case of a 45-year-old male surgeon who presented with a one-year history of episodic bilateral upper and lower limb weakness. Initial investigations, including brain and cervical spine MRI, were interpreted as consistent with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, for which treatment was commenced. Following a symptom-free interval after a one-month course of corticosteroids, the patient experienced a recurrence at eight months, prompting dynamic MRI of the cervical spine, which revealed a type C hypoplastic C1 posterior arch causing dynamic spinal cord compression during hyperextension. The diagnosis was revised accordingly. Supplementary investigations confirmed atlantoaxial stability and normal vertebral artery anatomy bilaterally. The patient provided consent and underwent posterior surgical decompression of the entire posterior arch, without instrumented fusion. Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring guided the extent of resection; decompression began on the fibrous left-sided arch, extending to the level of the vertebral artery groove, followed by the bony right-sided arch, sequenced to preserve facet joint integrity. The patient achieved complete symptom resolution postoperatively. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by symptomatic C1 arch hypoplasia, which may mimic demyelinating disease, and demonstrates that surgical decompression, guided by intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring and tailored to arch morphology, can achieve excellent neurological outcomes without the need for instrumented stabilisation.

title: Diagnostic Tools Used for Tuberculous Pleural Effusion and Their Association With Treatment Outcomes.
abstract: Background Tuberculous pleural effusion (TPE) is difficult to confirm because pleural disease is often paucibacillary. Pleural-fluid biomarkers, culture, molecular assays, and pleural biopsy can improve diagnostic certainty, but their availability varies substantially in resource-limited settings. Objective To describe the diagnostic investigations used for suspected TPE at AlShaab and Abu Anjaa Teaching Hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017, and assess their association with treatment outcomes. Methodology This retrospective cohort study included 69 patients with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of TPE at two teaching hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017. The first author collected demographic, clinical, investigation, treatment, and outcome data from patient records using a standardized data-collection checklist. Investigations were classified according to whether a test and result were documented. Associations with outcome were assessed using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Chest radiography was performed in 67/69 patients (97.1%). Pleural-fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) was recorded in 1/69 (1.4%), culture in 6/69 (8.7%), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 4/69 (5.8%), and pleural biopsy in 7/69 (10.1%). GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA) and pleural-fluid interferon-gamma testing were not performed. HIV testing was not documented in 50/69 patients (72.5%). Thirteen patients (18.8%) received antituberculous treatment without pleural-fluid or tissue testing. Five (38.5%) had a favorable outcome, and eight (61.5%) had an unfavorable outcome, including four subsequently diagnosed with malignant effusion and one death. Among 56 patients who underwent at least one pleural-fluid or tissue test, 39 (69.6%) had a favorable outcome. Any diagnostic testing was associated with higher odds of favorable outcome (OR 3.67, 95% CI 1.05-12.87; Fisher's exact P = 0.054), although the association did not cross the conventional statistical-significance threshold. Conclusions Confirmatory testing for suspected TPE was used inconsistently, while several clinically useful tests were rarely or never available. Patients treated without pleural-fluid or tissue testing had more unfavorable outcomes, including missed malignant effusion. The findings support a pragmatic minimum diagnostic bundle before prolonged empiric treatment, while recognizing that this observational study cannot establish that testing caused better outcomes.

title: A Case of Advanced Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Diagnostic Challenges and Sequential Systemic Therapy.
abstract: Advanced cutaneous malignancies with basaloid morphology can present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, particularly when pathological interpretations differ and disease progresses during systemic treatment. We describe the clinical course of a 53-year-old woman with an extensive, unresectable cutaneous tumor involving the posterior neck and occipital region, accompanied by bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and additional clinically suspected cutaneous deposits. The initial diagnosis was trichoblastic carcinoma, whereas expert pathological review favored basal cell carcinoma. The extent of disease precluded surgery and definitive radiotherapy. First-line vismodegib was initiated, and palliative radiotherapy delivering 30 Gy in 10 fractions to the occipital lesions and bilateral cervical lymph nodes was completed one year later. Clinical progression was documented three months after completion of radiotherapy; one month after this, MRI demonstrated extensive infiltration involving the left parotid gland and adjacent pharyngeal spaces. Second-line cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil were subsequently administered. Follow-up MRI six months after the earlier MRI demonstrated substantial tumor volume reduction. PET/CT three months later showed a heterogeneous response compared with a year earlier, including regression at several previously involved sites and newly apparent metabolically active right axillary lymph nodes. A subsequent biopsy was reported as basaloid carcinoma. The patient later experienced clinical deterioration, received one cycle of cemiplimab, and died before further treatment or response assessment. This case illustrates the importance of pathological clarification, longitudinal imaging, and careful interpretation of treatment response during sequential systemic therapy for advanced basal cell carcinoma.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Computed Tomography for Radiographically Occult Scaphoid Fractures and Concordance With Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fracture. Non-union and avascular necrosis are complications of a missed fracture. Therefore, if plain radiographs are normal and symptoms persist, further imaging such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often performed. Previous systematic reviews have largely compared their diagnostic accuracy indirectly using separate patient cohorts. Our objective is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of CT for occult scaphoid fractures in patients who underwent both CT and MRI following a negative or equivocal initial radiograph, and to assess concordance between CT and MRI findings. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. OVID MEDLINE, OVID Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from inception up to August 31, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled adults with clinically suspected scaphoid fracture and a negative or equivocal initial radiograph who subsequently underwent both CT and MRI. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2). Studies affected by partial verification or incorporation bias were excluded from quantitative synthesis. CT sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. Concordance between CT and MRI was reported using percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Six studies contributed to the primary pooled analysis of CT diagnostic accuracy, with one study reporting two CT readers. Using the first reader data from that study, alongside the five other studies, pooled CT sensitivity was 79% (95% CI 61.5-89.8%) and specificity was 94.4% (95% CI 82.1-98.4%). A sensitivity analysis using the second reader produced a sensitivity of 69.2% (95% CI 48.0-84.6%), with an unchanged specificity of 94.4% (95% CI 85.5-98.0%). Three studies provided CT-MRI concordance data; two demonstrated almost perfect agreement, with Cohen's kappa values of 0.91. The dual-energy CT study demonstrated lower concordance. Three studies used a reference standard independent of both CT and MRI and demonstrated mixed comparative findings. Overall, one study was judged to have low risk of bias, and seven were high risk of bias. In the included studies, CT demonstrated high specificity but more limited sensitivity for occult scaphoid fracture in paired CT-MRI cohorts. These findings align with existing literature reviewing unpaired data sets. Therefore, the findings suggest that CT remains a relevant alternative to MRI, especially in centres where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, or for surgical planning.

title: Rapidly Evolving Aphasia as a Diagnostic Clue in First-Episode Psychosis: A Case Report of Anti-NMDAR Encephalitis.
abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis frequently presents with isolated psychiatric symptoms indistinguishable from primary psychosis, delaying diagnosis. The authors have described a previously healthy 35-year-old woman admitted with abrupt first-episode psychosis, who (within 48 hours and without seizures, movement disorder, or altered consciousness) developed a true aphasic syndrome, fluctuating output with semantic and phonemic paraphasias and intermittent mutism, distinct from the disorganized speech of primary psychosis. The emergence of focal language disturbance prompted neurologic evaluation. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable; cerebrospinal fluid showed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and a raised immunoglobulin G index, with anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor immunoglobulin G strongly positive in cerebrospinal fluid. Pelvic imaging identified an ovarian teratoma, which was resected. First-line immunotherapy (intravenous methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin) followed by plasma exchange, with short-term antipsychotic treatment, achieved sustained remission. Serial neuropsychological assessment over 18 months documented a heterogeneous recovery trajectory: early, near-complete recovery of graphomotor speed and verbal consolidation, slower recovery of associative and working-memory functions, and verbal working memory persisting as the most stable residual deficit. This case showed that rapidly evolving aphasia, distinguished at the bedside from schizophasia, can localize an autoimmune process beyond any primary psychiatric differential and trigger the workup that secures the diagnosis.

title: Cystic Fibrosis
abstract: Clinical characteristics Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem disease affecting epithelia of the respiratory tract, pancreas, intestine, hepatobiliary system, and exocrine sweat glands. Morbidities include progressive obstructive pulmonary disease with bronchiectasis, recurrent sinusitis and bronchitis, exocrine pancreatic deficiency and malnutrition, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal manifestations (meconium ileus, rectal prolapse, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome), liver disease, diabetes, osteopenia/osteoporosis, male infertility due to hypoplasia or aplasia of the vas deferens, and reduced fertility or infertility in some women. By 2025, 95% of individuals with CF were eligible for targeted therapies, which has significantly altered the long-term course of the disease with a reduced overall disease burden. The impact is most evident in fewer hospitalizations, reduced clinic visits, and a decreased need for lung transplantation, all of which are associated with improved survival. While the CF disease phenotype has overall become less severe and more heterogenous in the era of highly effective CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy, pulmonary disease is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in CF. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of CF is established in a proband with (1) elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening, signs and/or symptoms suggestive of CF, or family history of CF; AND (2) evidence of an abnormality in CFTR function: sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L on sweat chloride testing, biallelic CFTR CF-causing pathogenic variants, or nasal transmembrane epithelial potential difference measurement consistent with CF. Management Targeted therapies: CFTR modulator therapy is available for individuals with responsive CFTR variants. These should be prescribed and managed by a clinician with CF expertise, particularly when initiating therapy. Supportive care: Newborns – management by a CF specialist or CF care center; airway clearance instruction; encouraging feeding with breast milk; routine vaccinations; contact precautions with every clinical encounter; antibiotics for bacterial suppression and treatment; nutrition management; pancreatic enzyme replacement; nutrient-dense food and supplements; fat-soluble vitamin supplements; laxative treatment as needed with surgical management for bowel obstruction; salt supplementation as needed. After the newborn period – airway clearance; pulmonary treatment (bronchodilator, hypertonic saline, dornase alfa, airway clearance, and aerosolized antibiotic); standard treatments for pneumothorax or hemoptysis; double lung transplant for those with advanced lung disease; routine vaccinations including influenza; contact precautions; antibiotics for bacterial suppression and treatment; antibiotics and/or surgical intervention for nasal/sinus symptoms; nutrition management; pancreatic enzyme replacement; nutrient-dense food and supplements; fat-soluble vitamin supplements; laxative treatment as needed with surgical management for bowel obstruction; standard treatments for gastroesophageal reflux disease; liver transplant when indicated; management of CF-related diabetes mellitus by an endocrinologist; assisted reproductive technologies (ART) for infertility; salt supplementation; standard treatments for associated mental health issues. Surveillance: Frequent assessment by a CF specialist to monitor for new or worsening manifestations; pulmonary function testing frequently after age five years; consider chest CT to assess for bronchiectasis every two years or as needed; cultures of respiratory tract secretions at least every three months; non-tuberculosis mycobacterium culture and measurement of serum immunoglobulin E annually or as indicated; annual complete blood count with differential; ENT assessment as needed; monitor growth and gastrointestinal manifestations at each visit; fecal elastase as needed; annual serum vitamin A, D, E, and prothrombin time (as a marker of vitamin K); colon cancer screening at least every five years beginning at age 40 years (beginning at age 30 years in transplant recipients); annual liver function tests; liver ultrasound with Doppler every two years starting at age three years; annual measurement of random blood glucose; annual two-hour glucose tolerance test beginning at age ten years; dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan in adolescence in those with risk factors for osteopenia, then every one to five years; infertility assessment as needed; annual electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine; annual assessment for depression and anxiety. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Environmental smoke and inhalants including electronic nicotine delivery products, exposure to respiratory infections, and dehydration. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Sweat chloride testing is recommended for all at-risk sibs of a proband to identify as early as possible those who should be referred to a CF center for initiation of early treatment. Genetic counseling CF is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a CFTR pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being heterozygous, and a 25% chance of inheriting neither of the familial pathogenic variants. Heterozygotes may be at increased risk for respiratory manifestations and/or pancreatitis. Once the CFTR pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, targeted heterozygote testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing for CF are possible.

title: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
abstract: Clinical characteristics Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is characterized by the association of gastrointestinal (GI) polyposis including distinctive arborized smooth muscle polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and cancer predisposition. PJS-type hamartomatous polyps are most common in the small intestine (in order of prevalence: jejunum, ileum, and duodenum), but can also occur in the stomach, large bowel, and extraintestinal sites including the renal pelvis, bronchi, gall bladder, nasal passages, bladder, and ureters. GI polyps can result in chronic bleeding, anemia, recurrent obstruction, and intussusception requiring repeated laparotomy and bowel resection. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation presents in childhood as dark blue to dark brown macules around the mouth, eyes, and nostrils, in the perianal area, and on the buccal intestinal mucosa. Hyperpigmented macules on the fingers and toes are common. The macules may fade in puberty and adulthood. Recognition of the distinctive skin manifestations is important, especially in individuals who have PJS as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant, as these skin findings often predate GI signs and symptoms. Individuals with PJS are at increased risk for a wide variety of epithelial malignancies (colorectal, gastric, pancreatic). Females are at risk for breast cancer, sex cord tumors with annular tubules (SCTATs), a benign neoplasm of the ovaries, and a gastric-type adenocarcinoma (adenoma malignum) of the cervix, a rare aggressive cancer. Males occasionally develop large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors of the testes, which secrete estrogen and can lead to gynecomastia, advanced skeletal age, and, ultimately, short stature if untreated. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of PJS is based on clinical findings. Identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in STK11 by molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and allows for testing of at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing. Management Treatment of manifestations: Routine endoscopic surveillance with polypectomy decreases the frequency of emergency laparotomy and bowel loss resulting from intussusception. Small bowel imaging includes video capsule endoscopy (VCE) and/or MRI enteroclysis. Magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) may be used if MRI is not tolerated, but MRE is less sensitive than MRI for polyps smaller than 1 cm. Balloon-assisted enteroscopy allows for removal of distal small bowel polyps. Occasionally intraoperative enteroscopy and enterotomy is needed for removal of large distal small bowel polyps. It is advised to remove polyps >15-20 mm or smaller if causing symptoms. Intussusception and malignancies should be treated in the standard manner. Surveillance: Surveillance in people with PJS is preferably done in a center of expertise. Children and adolescents – colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age eight years; if normal, resume GI surveillance at age 18 years and continue every one to three years. If polyps are detected at initial examination, repeat every one to three years based on size, number, and histopathology of polyps. Small bowel surveillance by VCE or MRI enteroclysis (or MRE if not tolerated) every one to three years based on findings beginning at age eight years. Examination for precocious puberty in females annually beginning at diagnosis or at least by age eight years. Testicular examination and examination for feminizing changes in males annually beginning at diagnosis or at least by age eight years through adulthood. Adults – colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, and small bowel examination by VCE or MRI enteroclysis (or MRE if not tolerated) every one to three years. Clinical breast examination in women every six to 12 months beginning at age 25 years; breast MRI with contrast in women annually from age 25 to 50 years (or if breast MRI with contrast is contraindicated or unavailable, breast ultrasound from age 25 to 30 years and mammography from age 30 to 50 years); consider tomosynthesis and ultrasound for those with dense breast tissue annually from age 30 to 50 years; mammography with consideration of annual breast contrast MRI for dense breasts every one to two years from age 50 to 75 years. Pelvic examination with pap smear and cytology (including those with negative HPV testing) in women annually beginning at age 25 years. Pancreatic imaging with endoscopic ultrasound or MRI is suggested annually beginning at age 40 years in a framework of a study or registry. For lung cancer, provide education regarding signs/symptoms of lung cancer and importance of smoking cessation. Testicular examination and examination for feminizing changes in males annually; testicular ultrasound for those with abnormal findings on examination. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Due to the increased risk for cervical, lung, and pancreatic cancer, smoking should be avoided. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Evaluate apparently asymptomatic older and younger at-risk relatives (including parents, sibs, and children) of an affected individual in order to identify as early as possible those who would benefit from initiation of surveillance, treatment, and preventative measures. If the pathogenic variant in the family is known, offer molecular genetic testing to at-risk relatives. If the pathogenic variant in the family is not known, offer clinical diagnostic evaluations. Genetic counseling PJS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most individuals diagnosed with PJS have an affected parent; some individuals represent apparently simplex cases and may have the disorder as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant. originalAbstract:
Clinical characteristics

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is characterized by the association of gastrointestinal (GI) polyposis including distinctive arborized smooth muscle polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and cancer predisposition. PJS-type hamartomatous polyps are most common in the small intestine (in order of prevalence: jejunum, ileum, and duodenum), but can also occur in the stomach, large bowel, and extraintestinal sites including the renal pelvis, bronchi, gall bladder, nasal passages, bladder, and ureters. GI polyps can result in chronic bleeding, anemia, recurrent obstruction, and intussusception requiring repeated laparotomy and bowel resection. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation presents in childhood as dark blue to dark brown macules around the mouth, eyes, and nostrils, in the perianal area, and on the buccal intestinal mucosa. Hyperpigmented macules on the fingers and toes are common. The macules may fade in puberty and adulthood. Recognition of the distinctive skin manifestations is important, especially in individuals who have PJS as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant, as these skin findings often predate GI signs and symptoms. Individuals with PJS are at increased risk for a wide variety of epithelial malignancies (colorectal, gastric, pancreatic). Females are at risk for breast cancer, sex cord tumors with annular tubules (SCTATs), a benign neoplasm of the ovaries, and a gastric-type adenocarcinoma (adenoma malignum) of the cervix, a rare aggressive cancer. Males occasionally develop large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors of the testes, which secrete estrogen and can lead to gynecomastia, advanced skeletal age, and, ultimately, short stature if untreated.

The diagnosis of PJS is based on clinical findings. Identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in STK11 by molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and allows for testing of at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing.

Balloon-assisted enteroscopy allows for removal of distal small bowel polyps. Occasionally intraoperative enteroscopy and enterotomy is needed for removal of large distal small bowel polyps. title: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen Syndrome
abstract: Clinical characteristics Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (JLNS) is characterized by bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vestibular dysfunction, and QTc prolongation on repeated testing. Iron deficiency anemia may be present in some people with KCNQ1 pathogenic variants. The hearing loss is most often congenital and severe to profound, although milder degrees of hearing loss have been described. Temporal bone anatomy on CT is normal. Vestibular dysfunction may result in gross motor delay (including later ages of walking), balance impairment, and absent physiologic nystagmus. In the absence of other reversible conditions that prolong the QT interval, serial 12-lead surface electrocardiograms show a prolonged QTc interval using the Bazzet formula exceeding 450 ms in prepubertal children, 460 ms in adult men, and 470 ms in adult women or a high probability long QT syndrome (LQTS) score ≥3.5. Repeated QTc prolongation must be observed, as a large overlap exists between unaffected individuals and those with LQTS. In KCNQ1-JLNS1, QTc prolongation is often severe (>500 ms) and associated with high risk for ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., torsade de pointes that can spontaneously resolve or degenerate into ventricular fibrillation), which if left untreated may result in syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD). In KCNE1-JLNS2, QTc prolongation is reported to be less severe, though significant risk for malignant ventricular arrhythmias remains. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of JLNS is established in a proband with congenital bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, electrophysiologic findings that meet diagnostic criteria for LQTS, and/or either biallelic KCNQ1 loss-of-function pathogenic variants or biallelic KCNE1 loss-of-function pathogenic variants identified by molecular genetic testing. Management Treatment of manifestations: Cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound bilateral SNHL, preferably done as soon as age six months and before age 12 months; hearing aids may be considered in those who have milder degrees of hearing loss or who are not candidates for cochlear implant; educational intervention for hearing loss; PT for gross motor delays; lifestyle modifications (avoiding QT-prolonging medication, correction and avoidance of electrolyte disturbance, and avoidance of sympathetic arousal) in those with QTc prolongation; non-selective beta-blockers (with consideration of mexiletine in those with KCNQ1-JLNS1) for long QT; left cardiac sympathetic denervation for symptomatic individuals when beta-blockers are not tolerated or are contraindicated at therapeutic doses, or for high-risk individuals; alternatively, implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) for symptomatic individuals despite beta-blocker therapy, or when beta-blockers are not tolerated or are contraindicated at therapeutic doses, and for individuals with prior cardiac arrest; standard treatment for iron deficiency anemia. Surveillance: Routine assessments per audiologist/otolaryngologist for SNHL with either a cochlear implant or amplification; assess gross motor skills every three months in infancy and every six to 12 months in childhood until PT/OT goals are met; consider annual assessment for changes in vestibular function; reassess cardiac findings including QTc monitoring and emergence of new manifestations at each visit; counsel and maintain lifestyle modifications at each visit; monitor adherence to doses and administration of prescribed medications, effectiveness and/or adverse effects of beta-blockers, and doses every three to six months during periods of rapid growth in children; evaluation of ICD at routine intervals or after ICD shock(s). Obtain complete blood count, iron studies, and gastrin levels as clinically indicated. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Perioperative precautions, including consideration of continuous heart monitoring during activation of cochlear implant; avoid drugs that prolong the QT interval; correct and avoid electrolyte abnormalities (specifically hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia); avoid sympathetic arousal triggers, such as high emotions, physical exercise, and swimming (during and while entering cold water); avoid physical activities that are known to precipitate syncopal events. Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is appropriate to evaluate all first-degree relatives of a proband with JLNS in order to identify as early as possible high-risk individuals (i.e., individuals with pathogenic variant[s] in KCNQ1 or KCNE1) who would benefit from intervention to prevent syncope, cardiac arrest, and sudden death. Assessment can include audiology examination to confirm congenital bilateral SNHL, repeated EKG assessment to establish the LQTS phenotype, and molecular genetic testing for the JLNS-related pathogenic variants identified in the proband. Perform clinical evaluation for LQTS in individuals who are heterozygotes for a KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variant. Pregnancy management: Medical therapy optimization and ICD implantation are recommended in pregnant women with LQTS who have experienced cardiac arrest, ventricular arrhythmias, and/or cardiac syncope despite beta-blocker therapy. Beta-blocker therapy should be continued in pregnant women with LQTS throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period, including during breastfeeding (i.e., until the child is weaned). Consultation with a fetal cardiologist should be performed early in pregnancy, as the fetus will have inherited one of the mother's KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variants. Fetal echocardiography is recommended to detect rhythm abnormalities, as fetal bradycardia is common in fetuses with LQTS. Genetic counseling JLNS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. At conception, each sib of an affected individual has a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being a carrier who may have long QTc only, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. When the KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

title: Lysosomal Acid Lipase Deficiency
abstract: Clinical characteristics The phenotypic spectrum of lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LAL-D) ranges from an infantile-onset form (previously known as Wolman disease) to childhood/adult-onset forms (previously known as cholesterol ester storage disease [CESD]). Infantile-onset LAL-D is rapidly progressive and symptoms arise within the first few days to weeks of life, with persistent vomiting, steatorrhea, and abdominal distention escalating (if untreated) to severe liver dysfunction and death within the first three to six months of life. However, with early diagnosis and initiation of treatment, long-term survival has improved significantly, although treated individuals may continue to have suboptimal growth, iron deficiency anemia, and lipid accumulation in the gastrointestinal mucosa. Those with infantile-onset disease who are treated typically experience normal long-term intellectual and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Individuals with childhood/adult-onset LAL-D typically present with otherwise unexplained transaminitis, organomegaly (splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly), and liver fibrosis that can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Childhood/adult-onset LAL-D does not affect long-term neurodevelopmental outcome. Affected individuals typically have hyperlipidemia, especially hypercholesterolemia. There is evidence to support efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy in stabilizing progression of liver fibrosis, reducing the need for lipid-lowering medications, and potentially lowering the risk of long-term cardiovascular complications. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of LAL-D is established in a proband with suggestive findings and biallelic pathogenic variants in LIPA identified by molecular genetic testing and/or deficient lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) enzyme activity in peripheral blood leukocytes or dried blood spots. Management Targeted therapies: For infantile-onset disease, enzyme replacement therapy with intravenous sebelipase alfa (premedication and desensitization protocols may be necessary) and total dietary fat restriction (total fat intake <1 g/kg/day) with supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids is recommended; some affected individuals may also benefit from hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. For childhood/adult-onset disease, intravenous administration of sebelipase alfa is recommended; dietary modification is not considered necessary, although some centers recommend dietary substrate reduction (restriction of dietary fat). Liver transplantation has been performed in individuals with adult-onset disease, especially in those with progressive liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, although there is a risk of recurrence of liver disease and it is not considered curative. Supportive care: Standard treatment for anemia/thrombocytopenia. For childhood/adult-onset disease, lipid-lowering medications for hyperlipidemia; standard treatment for cardiovascular disease, malabsorption/malnutrition, esophageal varices, and anemia/thrombocytopenia. Surveillance: For infantile-onset disease, measure weight, length/height, and mid-upper arm and abdominal circumference at each visit; assess for chronic diarrhea and monitor liver enzymes, essential fatty acids, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) levels every six months; obtain a complete blood count every six months in children and every six to 12 months in adults to assess for anemia and thrombocytopenia; monitor anti-drug antibody (ADA) concentration for those on enzyme replacement therapy if the ALT and AST levels are >3 times the normal limit or if there are clinical concerns regarding efficacy of treatment, such as weight loss / poor weight gain, increased stool frequency, or elevated inflammatory markers (i.e., ferritin and LDH); abdominal imaging to assess the liver, spleen, and mesenteric lymph nodes and to evaluate for adrenal calcifications and hepatocellular carcinoma every six to 12 months in those with advanced cirrhosis. For childhood/adult-onset disease, measure weight and length/height in infants/children and weight in adults at each visit; consider serial abdominal circumference in adults to assess for hepatosplenomegaly; assess for chronic diarrhea and monitor essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, and K) levels with consideration of monitoring liver enzymes, chitotriosidase, ferritin, and LDH as clinically indicated; measure liver enzymes every six to 12 months or as clinically indicated based on disease severity; assess for hepatomegaly, hepatic fibrosis, and cirrhosis at every visit, as indicated by clinical/biochemical parameters; monitor anti-drug antibody (ADA) concentration as clinically indicated for those on enzyme replacement therapy; obtain a complete blood count and fasting lipid levels every six months in children and every six to 12 months (or as clinically indicated based on disease severity) in adults; upper endoscopy every three years in those with severe liver disease; abdominal imaging to assess the liver, spleen, and mesenteric lymph nodes and to evaluate for hepatocellular carcinoma as clinically indicated in those with advanced cirrhosis. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Those with thrombocytopenia should avoid use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is appropriate to evaluate the sibs of a proband in order to identify those who would benefit from early institution of treatment. If the LIPA pathogenic variants in the family are known, molecular genetic testing can be used to clarify the genetic status of at-risk sibs; if the LIPA pathogenic variants are not known, assay of LAL enzyme activity can be used to assist in the identification of affected sibs. Genetic counseling LAL-D is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a LIPA pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. If the LIPA pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

title: Utility of Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy in Pediatric Gastrointestinal Disorders in Bangladesh: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Over the last few years upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy has been proven to be an effective diagnostic and therapeutic tool for various gastrointestinal diseases in children. This retrospective study was done in a tertiary care center of Bangladesh for one year to assess the indications of upper GI endoscopy including the diagnostic and therapeutic yields for various gastrointestinal disorders in children. During this period, 211 patients, aged ≤16 years, referred either from outpatient clinics or admitted inpatient wards were enrolled in study and their demographic data, endoscopic details (indications, findings and any complications) were collected and normal and abnormal endoscopic findings were compared. Mean age was found 9.5±3.5 years. The most common indication of upper GI endoscopy was recurrent abdominal pain (24.1%) followed by upper gastrointestinal bleeding (20.4%). Normal upper GI endoscopy was found in 74.51% of patients who had recurrent abdominal pain and oesophageal varices were found in 51.16% of patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding, endoscopic surveillance of oesophageal varices, foreign body ingestion and screening for oesophageal varix in chronic liver disease patient were significantly associated with abnormal upper GI endoscopy findings with p value 0.005, 0.001, 0.019 and 0.001 respectively. This study showed that recurrent abdominal pain was associated with normal upper GI endoscopy result in majority cases, so it should be reserved as second line investigation in patients with recurrent abdominal pain. However, every child with upper gastrointestinal bleeding should be evaluated by upper GI endoscopy. Upper GI endoscopy should be chosen in a justifiable way in paediatric population considering the signs and symptoms of disease.

title: Triphasic MRI evaluation of Hepatocellular Carcinoma according to ACR LI-RADS Compared with Histopathological Reports.
abstract: This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of ACR LI-RADS 5 on Triphasic MRI for detecting hepatocellular carcinoma, using histopathology as the reference standard. This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in the Department of Radiology and Imaging, Bangladesh Medical University (BMU), Dhaka, Bangladesh from April 2024 to September 2025. Patients with clinical, biochemical, or imaging suspicion of HCC underwent triphasic MRI and were categorized according to the ACR LI-RADS classification system. MRI findings were compared with histopathological diagnoses. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26.0 and statistical significance was considered at p<0.05. ACR LI-RADS 5 on triphasic MRI demonstrated a sensitivity of 83.33%, specificity of 91.67%, positive predictive value of 93.75%, negative predictive value of 78.57% and overall diagnostic accuracy of 86.67% for the detection of hepatocellular carcinoma. Triphasic MRI showed high diagnostic accuracy, specificity and positive predictive value of ACR LI-RADS 5 for detecting hepatocellular carcinoma, demonstrating strong agreement with histopathological findings and supporting its role as a reliable non-invasive diagnostic tool.

title: Diagnosis of Rhinoentomophthoromycosis in a 55 Years Old Male: A Case Report.
abstract: Entomophthoromycosis is a chronic fungal infection characterized by a diverse range of manifestations, including subcutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral infections. The majority of subcutaneous infections caused by entomophthoralean fungi are attributed to Basidiobolus spp, C. coronatus or C. incongruous. In this report, we present a case of rhinoentomophthoromycosis in a middle-aged, immunocompetent male, primarily affecting the nasopharynx. Initially, the diagnosis posed a dilemma, but it was ultimately confirmed through meticulous examination of microscopy and histopathology of the aspirate. The patient's response to antifungal therapy was favorable. We hereby provide a comprehensive account of this case and discuss the efficacy of Posaconazole in the treatment of rhinoentomophthoromycosis in a 55-year-old male patient with diabetes.

title: Radiographic Identification of Gold Threading: A clinical case study.
abstract: Dental hygienists play a crucial role in oral health care through the acquisition and interpretation of radiographs. Certain cosmetic facial procedures involving metallic materials may be visible on dental radiographs. These materials may obscure anatomical structures and complicate interpretation, which is essential for dental procedure treatment planning. The dental hygienist needs to be able to differentiate these artifacts from pathological conditions. This case study describes a 28-year-old female patient with intraoral and extraoral radiographs demonstrating thread-like radiopacities consistent with gold threading. This report highlights the radiographic characteristics of gold threading, outlines clinical implications, and emphasizes the importance of professional awareness of cosmetic facial procedures that may influence radiographic image interpretation and complicate accurate dental hygiene care planning.

title: Invasive cervical resorption: clinical management of necrotic pulp.
abstract: Invasive cervical resorption (ICR) is a pathologic and aggressive form of external root resorption that affects a small percentage of the population. Its etiology remains unclear and is considered multifactorial, involving trauma, orthodontic treatment, and internal bleaching, among other factors. This case report describes the clinical management of a patient diagnosed with class 3Ap ICR in the maxillary left canine. Cone beam computed tomography was crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. The treatment included endodontic therapy, surgical intervention, and restoration with bioactive resin containing surface-treated prereacted glass ionomer filler. Follow-up after 6 months showed clinical and radiographic treatment success, with no signs of recurrence. This report highlights the importance of early diagnosis and interdisciplinary management of ICR to preserve affected teeth and avoid extraction.

title: Clinical and <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT imaging features in a dog with bacterial sepsis of unknown origin.
abstract: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) imaging identified infection and inflammation earlier and with higher sensitivity than other imaging modalities in human medicine. A small case series explored the use of 18 F-FDG PET/CT for detecting the cause of fever of unknown origin in dogs. This report details clinical aspects and 18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging in the workup and treatment of a 12-year-old dog that was presented obtunded with severe neutropenia and hypoglycemia secondary to suspected sepsis. The 18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed moderate, patchy FDG avidity and soft-tissue swelling of the left carpus and tarsus (SUV max: 7.18 and SUV max: 5.58, respectively), moderate heterogeneous splenic and hepatic hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 3.42), and bilaterally symmetric renal hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 6.22) without appropriate flourine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) excretion. Other notable findings included marked, diffuse 18 F-FDG uptake within all bone marrow spaces (SUV max: 15.47) and a generalized, mild lymphadenopathy with moderate hypermetabolic activity. Positive blood cultures confirmed sepsis. Clinical deterioration despite appropriate antibiotic and supportive therapy prompted euthanasia. Necropsy revealed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic necrotizing vasculitis with thrombosis and necrosis in heart, spleen, brain, and liver, consistent with septicemia. Enterococcus faecium was isolated from lungs, kidneys, and spleen; Serratia marcescens was isolated from lungs and kidneys. This is the first documented report of the use of 18 F-FDG PET/CT for the diagnostic workup of a septic patient in veterinary medicine with corroborative necropsy findings to confirm PET/CT suspicion of disseminated septicemia. Key clinical message: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography imaging, which combines the functional, metabolic information from a PET scan with the high-resolution anatomical detail from a CT scan, should be considered as an adjunctive imaging modality for the diagnostic workup to identify focal and systemic infections in veterinary medicine. This is critical for immunocompromised animals in which timely and accurate diagnosis is of utmost importance, either for guiding case management and clinical outcome or for guiding owners through difficult decisions when the prognosis is guarded to poor.
